body_markdown:
A recent **Salmonella outbreak in the UK** has prompted renewed warnings for consumers to check the eggs they buy and take sensible food safety precautions. Health officials are investigating a rise in infections caused by a particular strain of *Salmonella Enteritidis* , with eggs imported from outside the UK being examined as a possible source.


The UK Health Security Agency identified an increase in cases in May 2026 after genetic testing showed that infections were being caused by the same strain. The investigation remains ongoing, and authorities have said there is currently no identified link between the outbreak and eggs or poultry produced in the UK.


One of the most important things consumers can do is understand the **British Lion egg mark** , which appears as a small Lion symbol stamped onto qualifying eggs.


## What is the British Lion egg mark?


The British Lion mark is a food safety assurance symbol used on eggs produced under the British Lion Code of Practice.


The scheme requires participating producers to follow detailed controls covering the egg production and supply chain. These include Salmonella vaccination for laying hens, enhanced hygiene measures, testing and traceability. The scheme is also independently audited.


More than 90 per cent of UK eggs are produced under the British Lion scheme, according to the organisation behind the programme.


For shoppers, the easiest way to check an egg is to look at the shell itself. A qualifying egg should carry the **Lion symbol alongside its identification code** .


The code can also provide information about the farming method, country of origin and individual farm. This means eggs can be traced through the supply chain if there is a food safety concern.


## Why are consumers being told to check their eggs?


The current investigation is focused on a rise in Salmonella infections across the UK. According to the UKHSA, the cases are associated with a single strain identified through whole genome sequencing.


The agency has said the outbreak may be linked to eggs imported from outside the UK, although investigations are continuing and the source has not been definitively established.


This distinction is important. A food safety investigation does not mean that every egg sold in British supermarkets is unsafe.


Instead, consumers should follow official advice, pay attention to product information and practise good kitchen hygiene.


The British Lion scheme is designed to reduce Salmonella risks through measures introduced throughout egg production. According to the scheme, participating hens are vaccinated against Salmonella, while eggs, hens and feed are subject to traceability requirements.


## How can you reduce the risk of Salmonella?


There are several straightforward steps households can take when handling and preparing eggs.


First, check the shell for the British Lion mark and make sure the egg is within its best-before date. British Lion eggs are date-stamped on the shell as well as being labelled on the carton.


Second, avoid using eggs that are dirty, cracked or broken. A damaged shell can make it easier for bacteria to enter the egg.


Third, wash your hands before and after handling eggs and clean kitchen surfaces and utensils after preparing food.


Cooking is also important. If you want to minimise the risk of Salmonella, cook eggs thoroughly until both the white and yolk are firm. This is particularly sensible when preparing food for people who may be more vulnerable to serious foodborne illness.


Raw mixtures such as cake batter should also not be tasted before cooking when using eggs that have not been specifically produced for raw consumption.


## What are the symptoms of Salmonella?


Salmonella infection can cause a range of gastrointestinal symptoms.


Common symptoms include diarrhoea, stomach cramps, vomiting and fever. Symptoms can vary from person to person and may become more serious in some cases.


Anyone who develops significant symptoms after eating potentially contaminated food should seek appropriate medical advice, particularly if symptoms are severe, persistent or accompanied by signs of dehydration.


People who are especially vulnerable to complications from foodborne infections should take extra care with food preparation and seek medical guidance if they become unwell.


## Does the Lion mark mean eggs are completely risk-free?


No food safety system can reasonably be described as eliminating every possible risk.


However, the British Lion scheme was created specifically to reduce the risk of Salmonella through vaccination, hygiene controls, testing, traceability and independent auditing. The Food Standards Agency previously recognised the improved safety record of British Lion eggs when updating its advice on eating runny eggs.


The key point for consumers is that the mark represents a particular production standard. It should not be confused with a guarantee that contamination is impossible.


Consumers should continue to follow normal food hygiene practices even when buying eggs carrying the Lion symbol.


## What should shoppers do now?


There is no need to panic or throw away every egg in your refrigerator simply because an outbreak investigation is underway.


Instead, check the shells of the eggs you have at home. Look for the British Lion mark and the accompanying code. Check the best-before date and avoid eggs with cracked shells.


If an official food recall is announced, follow the specific instructions from the relevant food safety authorities or retailer. A recall applies to particular products or batches, so consumers should not assume that all eggs are affected.


The safest approach is to stay informed, follow official guidance and maintain good food hygiene.


## The bigger picture


The current Salmonella investigation highlights why traceability and food safety controls are important. When the source of an outbreak needs to be identified, being able to track food through the supply chain can help investigators establish where contamination may have occurred.


For British Lion eggs, the production system includes identification and traceability measures designed to link eggs back through the supply chain.


For consumers, the message is relatively simple: **check the mark, handle eggs carefully and cook them properly when appropriate** .


The investigation into the current outbreak is continuing, so advice may change as authorities gather more evidence. Consumers should rely on updates from the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency and other official food safety bodies rather than social media claims or unverified reports.

If you are concerned about symptoms of Salmonella infection or believe you have eaten a recalled product, consult the appropriate health or food safety authority for current advice.
